Friday. Chandrika noticed the colony park was full of wrappers and old bottles. She told her friends on the swings. “Who will clean it?” asked Hrithik. “We will,” she said.
Saturday. Six children turned up with gloves and cloth bags. Two uncles brought sacks and showed them how to separate plastic. Hrithik carried the heaviest bag and puffed. A small boy named Anand held the bag open with both hands, silent and proud.
Sunday. The park looked different. A little girl swung on the swings and laughed. Chandrika stood at the gate and grinned. “We did that,” she said quietly.

qa.q: How many children came to clean the park on Saturday?
qa.a: Six children turned up with gloves and cloth bags.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel on Sunday when she saw the clean park?
qa.a: Chandrika felt proud. Standing at the gate and grinning, she quietly said that they had done it.

qa.q: What small step turned Chandrika's noticing into action?
qa.a: When Hrithik asked who would clean it, she said “we will” and invited her friends. That made it a shared job, not a complaint.

qa.q: How might Anand, who held the bag open, have felt?
qa.a: Anand probably felt proud to have a real job in the clean-up, since he held the bag with both hands, silent and proud.

grounding: Shows a child joining a clean-up drive with friends and feeling proud that together they made a difference.

passage:
Jahnavi, you asked why I keep this old school badge. Let me tell you. When I was ten, my class decided to collect used books for a village school. I’m Neelam, and I had never organised anything.
We borrowed a handcart. Ravi, the strongest boy, pulled it. A quiet girl, Divya, kept the list and ticked every house. I only knocked on doors and felt my knees shake.
By evening we had three hundred books. Our teacher looked at the cart and said nothing for a while. Then she smiled. Divya put her pencil behind her ear and we all laughed.

qa.q: What did Neelam's class collect?
qa.a: Neelam's class collected used books for a village school.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt knocking on doors?
qa.a: Neelam was nervous, since the knees shook. Neelam had never organised anything before but kept knocking on doors anyway.

qa.q: Which choice by the class made the collection succeed?
qa.a: They divided the jobs: Ravi pulled the cart, Divya kept the list and Neelam knocked on doors. Each child did the part that suited them.

qa.q: What might Divya have been feeling as she ticked every house on the list?
qa.a: Divya may have felt proud and focused, since her quiet job kept everyone's effort organised. Putting the pencil behind her ear at the end suggests a happy, satisfied mood.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood book drive with a class, where each child's small part added up to something real.

passage:
'Ew, a chips packet in the swing!' Harish held it up with two fingers.
'Bag!' Sachin held out the sack. 'That's thirty-one.'
'You're counting?'
'Obviously. Pooja didi said if we fill three sacks, the colony will buy a new see-saw.'
'Three?' Harish looked at the park, full of wrappers and broken bottles. 'That'll take forever.'
'Not if everyone helps.' Sachin pointed. Five more kids from Block B were coming with gloves, and old Mr Qureshi was carrying a rake.
'Leave the glass for me,' Mr Qureshi called. 'You do the paper.'
By evening they had four sacks. Harish sat on the swing, sweaty, looking at the clean grass. 'We did that,' he said.
'We did,' Sachin said. 'Next Sunday, the drain?'

qa.q: How many sacks did they fill by evening?
qa.a: Four sacks.

qa.q: How did Harish feel sitting on the swing at the end?
qa.a: Proud and satisfied, seeing the clean grass and knowing they had done it together.

qa.q: What made the clean-up work?
qa.a: Many people joining, a clear goal of three sacks, and Mr Qureshi handling the broken glass safely while the children picked up paper.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi feel helping the children?
qa.a: Pleased and involved, happy to see kids caring for the park and to keep them safe from the glass.

grounding: Children clean up a colony park together and feel proud that their small shared effort made a difference.

subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]
passage: When I was in Class 5, our teacher told us a village school near Mysuru had no library. I thought, what can kids do? But my friend Chetan made a big box with BOOKS PLEASE painted on it, and we put it at the school gate. Every morning I checked it. On day one there were two books. By day ten there were so many we needed three more boxes. I gave my favourite storybook, the one about the tiger, even though it hurt a bit. When we saw photos of the village children reading our books on the floor of their new library corner, my chest nearly burst. I'm Chandrika, and that's when I learned that small hands can do big things.

qa.q: What did Chetan paint on the box?
qa.a: BOOKS PLEASE.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel seeing the photos of the village children?
qa.a: So proud and happy that Chandrika felt ready to burst.

qa.q: What made the book drive succeed?
qa.a: A simple idea, a visible box at the gate, checking it daily and many families joining in over ten days.

qa.q: What might the village children feel when the books arrived?
qa.a: Excited and delighted to have a library corner and new stories to read.

grounding: A child joins a school book drive and feels proud that together the children made a real difference.

passage: Class 6 teacher's note, Friday. The blanket drive the class started for the night shelter has finished. Trisha and Gurleen came up with the idea after seeing people sleeping near the station. At first only four children brought blankets. Then Trisha made posters, and Gurleen visited other classes during break to explain. By Wednesday we had sixty-three blankets. Today, with parents' permission, six children came with me and the shelter manager to hand them over. Trisha held the list; Gurleen carried the biggest bag. On the bus back, Gurleen said, 'We're only kids, but we did this.' The whole group was glowing. Next week I will ask them to write about it for the school assembly.

qa.q: How many blankets had they collected by Wednesday?
qa.a: Sixty-three.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel on the bus back?
qa.a: Proud and happy, amazed that a group of kids had made a real difference together.

qa.q: What helped the drive grow from four blankets?
qa.a: Trisha's posters and Gurleen explaining the idea to other classes, so many more children joined in.

qa.q: How might the shelter manager see the children's visit?
qa.a: Probably touched and grateful, seeing children care enough to collect sixty-three blankets.

grounding: A teacher's note on children who ran a blanket drive together and felt proud of their shared difference.

passage:
Sunday
Dear Diary,
Today Jyoti, Pintu, six others and I cleaned the colony park! It was Jyoti's idea, because the slide was full of chips packets. Mrs Kapoor from B-block gave us gloves and big bags. I found a broken doll, forty-three wrappers (I counted) and one slipper. Pintu found a marble and said it was treasure. We filled eleven bags. My arms hurt. After lunch the little kids came, and the slide was shiny and nobody had to step over rubbish. Uncle from the ironing stall said, "Shabash, children." We're only nine kids, but the whole park looks new. Jyoti says next month the drain corner. I'm in.
Lakshmi 😊

qa.q: How many bags did the children fill?
qa.a: They filled eleven bags.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after the clean-up?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt proud and happy, arms aching, seeing the whole park look new 😊

qa.q: What helped the clean-up work?
qa.a: Jyoti had a clear idea, Mrs Kapoor gave gloves and bags, and nine children shared the work.

qa.q: What might the clean park mean for the little kids?
qa.a: They can play on a shiny slide without stepping over rubbish, which makes the park feel like theirs again.

grounding: Lakshmi's diary shows a child joining friends in a colony clean-up and feeling proud that together they made a difference.
